The river decision in a three-bet pot: value, bluffs and the final price

You three-bet to 10 BB, bet 5 BB on the flop, and bet again on the turn. The river pot is either 55.5 BB or 79.5 BB, depending on which turn size was called. With no sixth community card coming, should you check behind, make a value-bet hypothesis, try to bluff, or call when the cutoff leads? Reconstruct the river before choosing a story about the other player's hand.

Educational study away from live play. Every board, holding, action, response and opponent-range weight below is fictional. This is a six-handed, 100 BB effective no-limit Texas hold'em cash-game model with 0.5/1 BB blinds and no ante, straddle, rake, fees, side pot or tournament payout effects. The numbers are auditable chip accounting, not solved strategies, observed opponents, general-purpose bet sizes or guaranteed profitable actions. No gambling account or money is needed.

Pot ledgerTwo riversCheck or betBluff mathFacing a leadLarge river potFacing a raiseSelf-checks

1. Arrive at the river with one history, not an average pot

Carry forward the exact second-barrel example from the preceding lesson. Six players start with 100 BB each before posting. The small blind posts 0.5 and big blind posts 1. Under the gun and hijack fold. Cutoff (CO) raises to 2.5 BB total; button (BTN) three-bets to 10 BB total. Both blinds fold, and cutoff pays another 7.5 BB. The flop pot is 10 + 10 + 0.5 + 1 = 21.5 BB, with 90 BB behind each of the two remaining players.

Cutoff checks the flop, button bets 5 BB, and cutoff calls 5. The turn pot is 21.5 + 5 + 5 = 31.5 BB, and both players have 85 BB behind. Cutoff checks the turn. The button either bets 12 BB and gets called, or, in a separate hypothetical line, bets 24 BB and gets called. Do not combine the two bets into one hand. In either line the players' contributions remain equal, and cutoff acts first on the river.

Independent called-turn branches arriving at the river
Turn actionRiver pot before bettingEach stack leftRiver SPRLargest possible individual river bet
S: BTN bets 12 BB; CO calls 1231.5 + 12 + 12 = 55.5 BB85 − 12 = 73 BB73 / 55.5 ≈ 1.3273 BB, about 131.5% of pot
L: BTN bets 24 BB; CO calls 2431.5 + 24 + 24 = 79.5 BB85 − 24 = 61 BB61 / 79.5 ≈ 0.7761 BB, about 76.7% of pot

A smaller river SPR does not prove that a shove is warranted. It tells us what the remaining stack represents relative to the pot. The river is the final betting street; when action closes, there is a showdown or an uncontested pot. Cutoff acts first; button acts last if cutoff checks. If cutoff bets, button must respond with a fold, call or legal raise. A check is not available while facing an outstanding bet.

2. The same A♥ K♥ changes meaning on two different rivers

The following are alternative, independent fictional boards, not successive streets of the same hand. Button has A♥ K♥ in both solely to make card comparison easy. Each river is compatible with its four preceding community cards. The S and L accounting above could be applied to either board, but the strategic assumptions should not be copied across boards.

Board A: A♣ 7♦ 2♠ K♠, river 3♦

Five community cards

A♣7♦2♠K♠3♦

Button's A♥ K♥ is two pair, aces and kings, with a seven kicker (A-A-K-K-7). The river does not pair the board or complete a spade flush; a missed spade draw is possible, but neither player's exact range is known. A♦ Q♦ would be a worse pair of aces; 7♣ 7♥ would be a better set of sevens. Those are two legal example holdings, not assertions about what cutoff played.

Board B: 9♠ 8♠ 7♦ 6♠, river 2♦

Five community cards

9♠8♠7♦6♠2♦

Button's A♥ K♥ remains ace-high, with A-K-9-8-7 as its best five. Q♥ J♥ would be a worse high-card hand; T♥ 4♥ would make a ten-high straight using 6-7-8-9-T. A cutoff holding two spades would have a flush. There are only three spades on the board, so a single spade in the hole is not enough for a flush here.

One-card sensitivity check: if Board B's river had been T♠ instead of 2♦, the five board ranks 6-7-8-9-T would give everybody at least a ten-high straight, while the four spades on the board would let any player holding a spade make a flush. A jack without a spade could make a higher, jack-high straight. A♥ K♥ would play the board's ten-high straight, not remain ace-high. Do not reuse the Board B 2♦ showdown comparisons on that different river.

Board A's two pair and Board B's ace-high are specific made hands. Neither description alone tells you which opponent hands have survived a preflop call, a flop call and a turn call. The value-versus-bluff decision depends on the range after those actions. Use board reading and combination counting to distinguish a physically possible hand from an assumed frequent hand.

3. After cutoff checks, button may check behind or bet for a reason

Take only Branch S: 55.5 BB pot and 73 BB behind each. Cutoff checks the river. If button checks back, the river betting round closes at 55.5 BB, both retain 73 BB, and the remaining eligible players proceed to showdown. Checking does not fold the button's hand; it preserves whatever showdown share A♥ K♥ has against the actual, still-hidden cutoff cards. There is no sixth community card to receive for free.

Instead, suppose button bets 24 BB into the 55.5 BB pot, about 43.2% of pot. Cutoff now sees 55.5 + 24 = 79.5 BB in the middle and owes 24 more. A call creates 55.5 + 24 + 24 = 103.5 BB; both have 73 − 24 = 49 BB left. Under a heads-up, no-rake, no-ties chip model, if a call closes action, cutoff's break-even call share is 24 / 103.5 ≈ 23.19%. That is a price, not cutoff's measured chance of winning.

Branch S after cutoff checks on the river
Button action and cutoff responseContested pot at end of actionChips left, eachMeaning
BTN checks back55.5 BB73 BBShowdown; button keeps its possible share
BTN bets 24; CO folds55.5 BBBTN's 24 BB uncalled wager is returnedButton wins the pre-bet contested pot
BTN bets 24; CO calls 24103.5 BB49 BBShowdown after the completed call

Value-bet hypothesis on Board A: if cutoff checks and would call 24 BB often enough with worse aces, A♥ K♥ can gain from those calls. But some sets beat it, and worse hands might fold. Merely finding A♦ Q♦ as one possible worse call does not establish that betting is better than checking. You would need an evidence-based estimate of the actual calling and raising range, then compare the expected result with the check-back option. A river value bet does not deny a draw's future card; there is no future card.

Bluff hypothesis on Board B: A♥ K♥ is ace-high on 9♠ 8♠ 7♦ 6♠ 2♦. A bet might persuade some better one-pair hands to fold, but straights or flushes may call, and ace-high can itself beat other unpaired hands at showdown. Betting therefore sacrifices an uncertain but nonzero possible check-back value. “I missed, so I must bluff” is not a complete comparison. If the cutoff folds, the button's uncalled 24 BB is returned; do not count a 79.5 BB gross award and then also treat the 24 BB as a loss.

4. The bluff's fold threshold is not the caller's equity threshold

In a deliberately restricted pure-bluff model, suppose a bettor cannot win or tie when called, checking has zero value, a fold wins the existing pot and there are no fees or raises. If the pot before the bet is P and the bet is B, the bet breaks even against checking at a fold probability of B / (P + B). This formula measures an assumed bet's risk and reward; it does not forecast that anyone will fold. In our actual Board B example A♥ K♥ can beat some missed hands, so the pure-bluff premise is not established for that holding.

For the separate player facing a bet, the simplified showdown-call threshold is B / (P + 2B), because both the bettor's wager and the caller's payment enter the contested pot. The two denominators differ for a reason. The caller's fraction is a required pot share, not a fold frequency; the bettor's fraction is a required fold probability in a different hypothetical model.

Do not confuse the two different river percentages
Starting pot and hypothetical betPure zero-equity bluff break-even foldsOpponent's no-tie call-price thresholdPot after call
S: 24 into 55.5 BB24 / 79.5 ≈ 30.19%24 / 103.5 ≈ 23.19%103.5 BB
L: 61 into 79.5 BB61 / 140.5 ≈ 43.42%61 / 201.5 ≈ 30.27%201.5 BB

Neither column is a prescribed betting or calling frequency. If the bettor sometimes wins when called, or could win by checking, the comparison needs those payoff branches. A player can hold a blocking card that removes some opposing combinations, but blockers alone do not establish how often those combinations reach the river. In a real raked game the exact accounting must include the applicable deductions. For the general formulas, work through the bluff versus call-price distinction.

5. If cutoff leads, button has to evaluate a river call, not a free check

Return to Branch S and Board A's A♣ 7♦ 2♠ K♠ 3♦. Now change only the river action: instead of checking, cutoff bets 18 BB into 55.5 BB. Button still has A♥ K♥ and 73 BB behind before its response. The pot facing button is 55.5 + 18 = 73.5 BB. A call costs another 18, makes 73.5 + 18 = 91.5 BB, and leaves both players 73 − 18 = 55 BB. The simplified no-tie break-even call share is 18 / 91.5 ≈ 19.67%.

Button cannot check behind while facing 18. It can fold, call or make a legal raise. A call ends the final betting action and immediately leads to showdown; it cannot improve A♥ K♥ with a sixth card or make cutoff fold. An 18 BB river lead is not automatically a weak “block bet,” strong value or a bluff. Those labels require reasoning about what the cutoff is betting, and why, after calling the previous streets.

Two explicitly fictional holdings, two assumed mixtures

For a deliberately narrow teaching calculation, imagine cutoff's entire river betting range contains only 7♣ 7♥ (a set beating A♥ K♥) and Q♠ J♠ (a missed spade draw that A♥ K♥ beats). Each is compatible with Board A and button's cards. This is not a credible complete preflop or turn range, and the weights below are invented to show sensitivity, not estimated population or solver frequencies.

If the missed-draw hand accounts for an assumed 25% of bets, calling has conditional chip EV of 0.25 × 91.5 − 18 = +4.875 BB relative to folding at this decision. If only 10% are missed-draw bets, the same call is 0.10 × 91.5 − 18 = −8.85 BB. The pot price stays 19.67% in both worlds. What changed was the unverified opponent mixture, not the arithmetic.

A♥ K♥ is not necessarily a pure bluff catcher against a realistic river bet, because some worse made hands may also bet. A true bluff catcher is defined relative to a specified betting range: it beats that range's bluffs but loses to its value hands. This two-holding teaching model has that simplified shape, but it cannot justify a real-world call until one explains why each holding would have reached the river and bet. The beginner river-call lesson covers the vocabulary; range combinations addresses card removal.

6. Branch L is a different river: 61 BB behind, not 73

Return to the other turn line, 24 BB bet and call, and do not carry over the 12 BB ledger. The river begins with 79.5 BB in the pot and 61 BB behind each. If cutoff checks, button can check behind to contest 79.5 BB at showdown, bet some lesser legal amount, or bet its entire 61 BB stack. A full-stack bet is approximately 61 / 79.5 ≈ 76.7% of the pot. This is a legal hypothetical amount, not a recommendation to shove A♥ K♥ on either board.

If button bets 61 and cutoff folds, the uncalled 61 BB is returned to button and button wins the original contested 79.5 BB. If cutoff calls 61, the pot becomes 79.5 + 61 + 61 = 201.5 BB, with neither player having chips behind. That total makes sense: the two opponents each began with 100 BB and the folded blinds supplied 1.5 BB. Cutoff needs a simplified no-tie pot share of 61 / 201.5 ≈ 30.27% to break even on the call versus folding. No further raise is possible against a fully all-in bettor with equal starting stacks.

Compare the two rivers honestly: the smaller turn barrel left a larger river stack relative to its pot, while the larger turn barrel left a more natural sub-pot-sized all-in amount. Neither fact proves which turn size or river action is more profitable. On Board A the two-pair holding could confront sets and worse aces; on Board B the ace-high holding could confront missed hands, straights and flushes. Changing the river board or the opponent's assumed reach distribution can reverse the value of checking, betting or calling.

7. A river raise still requires an incremental payment

For one last independent branch, return to S: 55.5 BB and 73 BB each. Cutoff checks; button bets 24; cutoff check-raises to 60 BB total on the river, instead of folding or calling. The minimum normal full raise over a 24 BB bet would be to 48 BB total, so 60 BB is a legal raise with 73 BB available. The pot when action returns to button is 55.5 + 24 + 60 = 139.5 BB.

Button already invested 24 on this river and owes 60 − 24 = 36 BB more to call. If button calls, the final pot is 55.5 + 60 + 60 = 175.5 BB, and each player has 73 − 60 = 13 BB unspent. That 13 is no longer playable in this hand because river betting is over after the call. Under the same closed-action, no-fee, no-tie model, the incremental call requires 36 / 175.5 ≈ 20.51% average pot share. A fold does not add the 36; a legal further raise would require a new branch.

Notice that the 20.51% price can be smaller than the 23.19% price against the initial 24 BB bet, even though a raise may represent a different, often stronger selection of hands. The mathematics becomes more favorable while the range could become less favorable. Do not mistake a cheaper percentage for a better call. See raise-to versus amount-owed accounting for the general rule.

8. A usable river decision memo separates four questions

Review questions worth writing before deciding if a river line is best
QuestionWhat can be checkedWhat cannot be inferred from pot size
What reached the river?Positions, exact preflop, flop and turn actions, stack changes and river cardA complete opposing range or exact prior frequencies
What happens if I check?Whether action closes, known showdown hand and remaining potGuaranteed defeat merely because a draw missed
What happens if I bet?Size, maximum legal stack, call amount and final potWhich worse hands call or better hands fold often enough
What happens if I face a bet?Incremental call price, pot share needed, legal responsesA bluff percentage, because a bluff is physically possible
Does a reference apply?Game type, effective stacks, rake, ranges, available bet sizes and boardA solver's answer from a different tree or an anecdotal opponent read

A clear review is allowed to end with “the call costs 18 BB and requires about 19.67% pot share, but the betting range is uncertain.” That is more useful than assigning a precise optimal frequency to an unsolved hand. GTO Wizard's custom-solution documentation shows how stack, range, rake and size choices alter an analysis. No solution has been run for these boards here, and no outside article's strategy frequencies have been attributed to them.

9. Seven self-checks: close the answers before you open them

CO checks, BTN bets 5 on the flop and CO calls. BTN then bets 12 on the turn and CO calls. How big is the river pot, and who acts first?

55.5 BB; cutoff acts first. Start from 21.5 BB after the preflop three-bet, add 5 + 5 on the flop, then 12 + 12 on the turn. Each has 73 BB left. A 24 BB turn bet belongs to the different 79.5 BB branch.

On 9♠ 8♠ 7♦ 6♠ 2♦, what is A♥ K♥? Would one spade in another player's hand make a flush?

Ace-high; no. The best five are A-K-9-8-7. Only three spades lie on the board, so two spades in the hole are needed for a completed flush. A ten makes a straight. If the river were T♠ instead, there would be a straight on the board and four board spades, a different hand entirely.

After the 12 BB turn call, cutoff checks the river and button bets 24. What does cutoff pay to call, and what is the final pot?

24 BB to call; 103.5 BB final pot. Before the river the pot is 55.5 BB. It becomes 79.5 after the bet and 103.5 after the call. The simplified no-tie break-even call share is 24 / 103.5 ≈ 23.19%, not 24 / 79.5.

In that same 55.5 BB river pot, does a 24 BB pure bluff need 23.19% folds?

No: 30.19% folds in the specified zero-showdown-value, zero-check-value model. The pure-bluff break-even fraction is 24 / (55.5 + 24) = 24 / 79.5. The 23.19% fraction prices the opponent's call, not the bettor's risk. Neither number is an estimated response frequency.

Cutoff leads 18 into 55.5 on the river. Can button check, and what is the price if button calls?

Button cannot check. Calling costs 18 and makes a 91.5 BB pot, with 55 BB behind each. The no-tie call-price threshold is 18 / 91.5 ≈ 19.67%. The real call still depends on which hands cutoff bets.

Button shoves the remaining 61 BB into the 79.5 BB river pot. If cutoff calls, what is the final pot and what happens to the uncalled amount if cutoff folds instead?

A call makes 201.5 BB, with no chips behind. The call threshold is approximately 30.27%. If cutoff folds, button's unmatched 61 BB is returned and button wins the 79.5 BB pre-bet pot; it does not win 140.5 BB plus keep the 61 BB as a separate profit.

Button bets 24 into 55.5, cutoff raises to 60 total. Does button owe 60 more and must button call because the price is 20.51%?

Neither. Button owes 60 − 24 = 36 BB more. Calling creates 175.5 BB and a 36 / 175.5 ≈ 20.51% direct-showdown threshold. That arithmetic does not establish the button's equity against a check-raising range. Folding or a legal further raise remains a separate decision.

10. Record an honest river review after the hand

  1. Fix the state: cash or tournament, seats, posted blinds, effective stacks, all preflop amounts as totals, every flop and turn bet, and which river pot branch actually happened.

  2. Show all five cards: write ranks and suits, your actual best five, alternative possible opposing hands and relevant blockers, without pretending those hands were observed.

  3. List legal actions: if the first player checked, the in-position player can check behind or bet. If facing a wager, separate fold, call and legal raise. The final call cannot purchase another card.

  4. Count chips: pot before the river, bet size, pot facing a response, incremental call, final contested pot, uncalled amount returned if applicable, and stacks after any call.

  5. Separate facts from models: record only observed action as fact, label hypothetical value/bluff hands and their weights, and note whether rake, ties, raises or prior-range assumptions alter the simplified calculations.

  6. Explain the uncertainty: say what credible evidence would move the decision, or mark it unresolved. A real hand history can be useful without claiming the line is solver-approved or profitable.
